etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English calm, calme, from Middle French calme, probably from Old Italian calma, of uncertain origin. Calma may derive from Late Latin cauma (“heat of the midday sun”), from Ancient Greek καῦμα (kaûma, “heat, especially of the sun”), from καίω (kaíō, “I burn”), or possibly from Latin caleō. Compare also Lombardic *chalm, *chalma (“frozenness”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *kalmaz (“frozenness, cold”).

Displaced native Middle English smilte (“quite, still, gentle”) from Old English smylte (“quiet, tranquil, calm, serene”).

definitions.definition: (of a person) Peaceful, quiet, especially free from anger and anxiety.
(of a place or situation) Free of noise and disturbance.

quote.citation: 1850, [Alfred, Lord Tennyson], In Memoriam, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, Canto XI:
quote.text: Calm is the morn without a sound,⁠Calm as to suit a calmer grief,⁠And only thro’ the faded leafThe chestnut pattering to the ground: […]

definitions.definition: (of water) with few or no waves on the surface; not rippled.
(in a person) The state of being calm; peacefulness; absence of worry, anger, fear or other strong negative emotion.

quote.citation: 1850, [Alfred, Lord Tennyson], In Memoriam, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, Canto XI:
quote.text: Calm on the seas, and silver sleep,⁠And waves that sway themselves in rest,⁠And dead calm in that noble breastWhich heaves but with the heaving deep.

definitions.definition: (in a place or situation) The state of being calm; absence of noise and disturbance.
A period of time without wind.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Mark 4:39:
quote.text: The wind ceased, and there was a great calm.

quote.citation: 1851 November 14, Herman Melville, chapter 64, in Moby-Dick; or, The Whale, 1st American edition, New York, N.Y.: Harper & Brothers; London: Richard Bentley, →OCLC, page 324:
quote.text: It was a calm ; so, forming a tandem of three boats, we commenced the slow business of towing the trophy to the Pequod.

quote.citation: 1697, Virgil, “(please specify the book number)”, in John Dryden, transl., The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Æneis. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: to calm the tempest raised by Aeolus
